September 10, 2026
Democratic U.S. Sen. John Fetterman made a surprise video appearance Wednesday at the GOP convention in Dallas, praising Republican Sen. Dave McCormick while vowing the pair of Pennsylvanians would continue working with President Donald Trump to "defend the steel way of life right here in the Steel Valley."
The brief, prerecorded appearance, which wasn't advertised on the convention's schedule, showed a deepening rift between Fetterman and mainstream Democrats. The video boosted speculation that Fetterman could switch parties.
MORE: Vivid Seats manipulates customers into paying more for tickets, Pa. prosecutors allege in lawsuit
"Yes, I'm a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I'm a common-sense Democrat," Fetterman said in the video, where he stood in front of a U.S. Steel mill in Braddock, Pennsylvania, roughly 10 miles outside Pittsburgh.
Fetterman also distanced himself from a wave of progressive Democrats, some affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America, who have won primaries this year.
"I'm always going to stand with America," he said. "I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life."
In addition to a more ideological divide with Democrats over issues such as Fetterman's strong support for Israel amid the continuing war in Gaza, Fetterman has taken heat from former aides who told the Wall Street Journal that he is indifferent toward his job.
Wednesday's video introduced McCormick before the GOP senator took the convention stage.
Fetterman lauded McCormick as "the kind of senator that gets the job done" and is "going to fight for Pennsylvania."
"I have this opportunity to introduce this great American, a great senator, and yes, he's in a different party, but I'm proud to count him as my great friend," he added.
Democratic members of Congress criticized Fetterman's cameo at the convention.
"A year ago I labeled John Fetterman 'Trump’s favorite Democrat,'" U.S. Rep. Brendan Boyle, a Pennsylvania Democrat, posted to social media. "Tonight, he yet again proves why."
Delaware Democratic U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride compared Trump’' presidency to a historic disaster.
"Being a Democratic politician who decides to speak at Trump's midterm convention is like boarding the Titanic after it hit the iceberg," she wrote.

Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman has faced intense criticism from Democratic Party figures and progressive activists after making a surprise virtual appearance at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas.
The Democratic senator used the video address to praise his Republican counterpart, Senator Dave McCormick, and signal his willingness to work with US President Donald Trump on industrial policy. The move triggered an immediate backlash within his own party, according to a report by The Hill.
Fetterman delivered the approximately one-minute address virtually while standing outside a major steel-processing facility in Pittsburgh. Wearing his trademark casual clothing, he described himself as a “common sense Democrat” and sought to distance himself from what he characterised as the extremes within his party.
He also praised McCormick as a close friend and said he intended to work to protect the US steel industry alongside Trump.
Fetterman’s appearance was greeted enthusiastically by conservative delegates at the convention. His willingness to praise a Republican senator and express support for working with Trump was viewed by attendees as evidence of bipartisan cooperation.
Within Democratic circles, however, the reaction was sharply different.
Party leaders and progressive activists quickly condemned the senator's decision to appear at the Republican gathering. Some of the strongest criticism came from Pennsylvania state Representative Malcolm Kenyatta, who issued a particularly harsh rebuke of Fetterman's address.
According to statements published by news agencies, Kenyatta remarked, “John Fetterman is the laziest Benedict Arnold America has ever seen. He didn’t even have it in him to get off his couch in his million-dollar penthouse to kiss Donald Trump’s ring in person. He phoned it in, just as he has every day as our senator. John should do his job or resign.”
Political analysts and commentators have also questioned whether Fetterman's increasingly independent positioning reflects the priorities of the voters who sent him to the US Senate.
The controversy has highlighted broader tensions within the Democratic Party as it attempts to preserve its coalition ahead of the crucial 2026 midterm elections.
With control of the US Senate expected to be closely contested, strategists are examining whether Fetterman's increasingly conservative rhetoric could further distance him from Democratic voters or create problems for the party's efforts to retain or expand its Senate numbers.
Fetterman's supporters argue that reaching beyond the traditional Democratic base and appealing to independent and cross-party voters can be crucial in politically competitive states such as Pennsylvania.
Critics, however, say publicly embracing Republican politicians and echoing elements of the Trump administration's message could weaken Democratic unity and undermine the party's broader legislative strategy.
The dispute reflects a larger debate within the Democratic Party over how far its candidates should move toward the political centre as they seek to compete in battleground states.

Sen. John Fetterman has once again angered the Democratic Party base with a stunt he pulled Wednesday evening.
Fetterman, D-Pa., made an unexpected appearance at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, delivering a prerecorded message praising President Donald Trump and his Pennsylvania counterpart, Republican Sen. Dave McCormick, while distancing himself from what he described as political “extremes and socialism” of his party.
Fetterman appeared in a roughly one-minute video that was played before McCormick took the stage at the Republican National Committee’s midterm gathering.
“Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said.
“I’m always going to stand with America,” he continued. “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life.”
Standing in front of a Pennsylvania steel mill, Fetterman used much of the message to highlight his relationship with McCormick and their shared interest in the state’s steel industry.
He described McCormick as a “great American” and praised him as “the kind of senator that gets the job done.”
Fetterman also said he intended to continue working with both McCormick and Trump on policies aimed at protecting steel production in Pennsylvania.
“I will work with President Trump to fight and defend the steel way of life,” Fetterman said.
The appearance was striking because Fetterman remains a Democratic senator and was speaking to an audience gathered specifically to help Republicans retain control of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The Dallas convention is an unusual off-year national gathering organized around Trump and Republican congressional candidates. Trump delivered the keynote address Wednesday night, while Vice President JD Vance and other Republican officials were also scheduled to appear during the two-day event.
Fetterman did not announce a party switch or formally endorse the Republican Party.
Instead, his remarks were framed around his relationship with McCormick and his continuing criticism of the Democratic Party’s left-wing socialism.
SHOCKING MOVE: Democratic Sen. John Fetterman makes a surprise video appearance at the GOP midterm convention, declaring he will reject “the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life.”
The appearance is a stunning turn for the first-term senator who skipped his… pic.twitter.com/dnbPPapjh0
— Fox News (@FoxNews) September 9, 2026
That distinction is consistent with Fetterman’s position over the past several years.
Since entering the Senate in 2023, he has repeatedly broken with fellow Democrats on several high-profile issues, particularly Israel, immigration and national security. He has been one of the Democratic Party’s strongest supporters of Israel and has sharply criticized some progressive activists and politicians associated with the Democratic Socialists of America.
Fetterman has also crossed party lines on a number of Senate votes.
Reuters noted that he supported multiple Trump administration nominees, opposed efforts to curtail U.S. military involvement in the conflict with Iran and repeatedly voted with Republicans during last year’s government shutdown.
Those positions have increasingly strained his relationship with parts of the Democratic Party.
The divide widened further in recent days after The Wall Street Journal reported complaints from former aides about Fetterman’s attendance at constituent meetings, Senate hearings and Pennsylvania events.
Several Pennsylvania Democrats responded publicly to that reporting, with some questioning Fetterman’s performance in office and his future within the party.
Fetterman has disputed that broader characterization of his work and has said he remains committed to representing Pennsylvania.
He has also repeatedly denied suggestions that he plans to become a Republican.
The relationship between Fetterman and McCormick has attracted attention since McCormick entered the Senate in 2025.
Although the two represent opposing parties, they have frequently emphasized areas of cooperation and have appeared together at events in Pennsylvania.
Fetterman has described McCormick as a friend, while McCormick has similarly spoken positively about their working relationship.
Their cooperation has been particularly visible on issues involving Pennsylvania’s industrial economy and U.S. Steel.
Fetterman has long argued that domestic steel production is important to western Pennsylvania communities, and his convention video used the mill setting to reinforce that message.

Today, we’re diving into John Fetterman’s peculiar RNC appearance, which we watched as a group last night. We also have a Treasury Department announcement to buy back debt and a reader question about sanctions on Russian oil. Plus, Ari, Kmele, and I recorded an in-person podcast ruminating on the 25th anniversary of September 11 and the seventh anniversary of Tangle.
There’s a lot to cover. It’s a 14-minute read.

Today’s topic.
John Fetterman. On Wednesday, Sen. John Fetterman (D-PA) appeared via video at the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention, reiterating his opposition to socialism and praising Sen. Dave McCormick (R-PA). Fetterman has frequently criticized the Democratic Party’s embrace of democratic socialism and anti-Israel rhetoric, leading to speculation that he could switch parties or become an independent.
Back up: In Pennsylvania’s 2022 Senate election, Fetterman defeated now-Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz on a platform of eliminating the filibuster, raising the minimum wage, and codifying abortion rights. Fetterman suffered a stroke during the campaign and spent three months recovering. Shortly after joining the Senate, he was hospitalized with clinical depression for a month and a half, rejoining the chamber in April 2023.
Fetterman has been an outspoken advocate for Israel, particularly in defense of its military response to Hamas’s October 7 attacks. He has also decried Democratic politicians’ criticism of the country, saying in July that he would only leave the Democratic Party if it became “the anti-Israel party.” Additionally, Fetterman has broadly backed U.S. military operations in Iran, repeatedly voting against war-powers resolutions to restrict President Donald Trump’s authority in the conflict.
Separately, recent reporting has highlighted staff turnover within Fetterman’s office and questions about his constituent services. Citing the senator’s former staff members, The Wall Street Journal reported last week that he has withdrawn from public commitments and frequently skips Senate votes while showing increased interest in appearing on conservative media programs. Fetterman said the report was “stripped of any context and circumstance” and based on “lies, half-truths, innuendos, [and] smears” from “disgruntled staffers.”
In his pre-recorded video for Wednesday’s GOP convention, Fetterman called himself a “common-sense Democrat” who will “always… stand with America.” In a statement afterward, he emphasized that he intends to remain in the party and fulfill his campaign promise of being Democrats’ “51st vote” in the Senate.
A New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena poll in August found that 22% of the state’s registered Democratic voters view him favorably, while 73% of Republicans do. Last week, former Rep. Conor Lamb (D-PA) called on the senator to resign, and Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-PA) said Fetterman is a “disgrace,” adding, “Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job.” Meanwhile, Sen. McCormick thanked Fetterman for his support and said, “We were both sent to Washington to fight for what’s best for PA.”
Today, we’ll share views from the right and left about Fetterman’s future. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul gives his take.
- Many on the right say Democrats are attacking Fetterman because he challenges party orthodoxy.
- Some argue the senator should switch parties.
- Others suggest Fetterman could complicate the post-midterms picture.
The Wall Street Journal editorial board wrote “Democrats want John Fetterman ‘on a pike.’”
“Sources who decline to be identified say [Fetterman] neglects semiofficial duties such as constituent meetings, committee hearings and public funerals, but that he appears on cable-news shows with regularity (including, mortal sin, Fox News),” the board said. “Mr. Fetterman’s real offense is political. He’s a consistent progressive on taxes, healthcare, climate, guns, social issues and much else. But he vocally supports Israel in its war against Hamas and Hezbollah, backs President Trump’s war in Iran, and rejects such progressive-left follies as abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and defunding the police.
“Such heterodoxy probably benefits Democrats by making their party seem less crazy. A lot of thanks he gets — his Democratic colleagues evidently want to ruin him,” the board wrote. “[Democrats will] feign indignation about poor office behavior, but what angers them is his occasional votes with Republicans, his refusal to indulge in hysteria about Mr. Trump and, especially, his unapologetic support for Israel. This is intolerable in today’s Democratic Party.”
In The Washington Examiner, Zachary Faria argued “by 2028, Fetterman can be a Democrat or a senator, but not both.”
“Fetterman will almost certainly face some socialist affiliated candidate [in 2028]. He or she will call Fetterman a closet Republican and accuse him of supporting the ‘genocide’ of Palestinians, and with Fetterman’s low scores among Democratic voters, he will lose, regardless of how much help [Senate Minority Leader Chuck] Schumer provides him,” Faria said. “That leaves Fetterman with two options going forward. The one he insists on holding to thus far is going down with the ship, accepting the fight in the Democratic Party, and, as a result, being out of office by January 2029.”
“Or Fetterman could jump ship and join the Republican Party, an idea that has been discussed louder in political circles as 2028 approaches. He is already extremely popular among Republicans, and a double-digit favorability among independents means he would be the heavy favorite to beat anyone (of either party) in a general election,” Faria wrote. “If he wants to choose the latter, he is running out of time… Republicans like him as a Democrat, but the standards change if he becomes a Republican. He would have GOP goodwill, but he would need to polish some Republican credentials as well.”
In The American Conservative, Spencer Neale discussed “the GOP’s John Fetterman wildcard.”
“As November heaves into view, Democratic capture of the Senate — an idea that seemed implausible at the beginning of this year — is also firmly in play… There is, as it turns out, an interesting wrinkle. If Democrats win with a razor-thin majority, there might be one man capable of denying them actual control: John Fetterman,” Neale said. “Fetterman has been a fervent supporter of the Iran War, for example, and a constant critic of his Democratic colleagues on foreign policy. The freshman senator from Pennsylvania has appeared on Fox News 56 times since the beginning of 2026, mostly to talk up Israel, lambast Islamist terror, and decry progressive Democrats.”
“Democrats don’t even control the Senate right now, yet Fetterman has single-handedly sunk Iran war powers votes at least four separate times since February. In a Senate under narrow Democratic control, Fetterman’s support for Trump’s wars could continue to kill his party’s efforts to wind these up,” Neale wrote. “After his humble beginning as a Bernie-bro-style populist, Fetterman has merrily morphed into a DINO (Democrat in Name Only)… Even if things go swimmingly in the midterms, Democrats could wake up in January with a majority in name but not in fact — all thanks to John Fetterman.”
- The left is critical of Fetterman, saying he has deceived his voters.
- Some suggest the party should ignore the senator.
- Others argue Fetterman leaving the Democratic Party would be a net positive.
The Philadelphia Inquirer editorial board detailed “what John Fetterman forgot about his U.S. Senate seat.”
“[Fetterman’s] supporters do deserve to be dismayed… at their increasingly right-leaning senior senator’s self-indulgent recent threats to leave the Democratic Party entirely. Fetterman won a competitive race as a Democrat thanks to voters who believed in him and his politics even after a stroke forced him off the campaign trail for months,” the board said. “Fetterman is making a very inside-the-Beltway mistake. Judging by his willingness to change his positions and party at a whim, he seems to think the Senate seat belongs to him rather than the people he represents.”
“Despite Fetterman’s proclaimed ‘moral clarity’ on Israel, he often speaks of his grievances with his fellow partisans — and his appreciation for Trump — in political rather than policy terms. He has groused about the repercussions of left-leaning Democrats’ positions for swing-state politicians like him, enthused about Trump’s sheer political talent, and lamented the electoral fate of Democrat Bob Casey, his former Senate colleague,” the board wrote. “Maybe the senator’s red shift is motivated less by foreign policy than by an impulse to keep his job — even if it means betraying his voters.”
In USA Today, Chris Brennan wrote “Democrats have a Fetterman problem. Or do they?”
“For more than a decade, Fetterman mostly provoked anger among Republicans. But now, like a professional wrestler after a ‘heel turn,’ Fetterman has his own party frothing as he cozies up to President Donald Trump,” Brennan said. “Do Democrats have a Fetterman problem? And, if so, what if anything should the party do about it? Here's an idea: Let Fetterman be Fetterman. Don't bite his outrage bait. Focus on the midterms. Pay him no attention at all.”
“Fetterman has a problem. His 2022 campaign was fueled by millions of dollars in small-donor campaign contributions from progressives who embraced his populism. That base has walked away. And those voters are not coming back. No wonder he feels a kinship with Trump, who has left parts of his MAGA base feeling infuriated and betrayed by the very actions Fetterman supports,” Brennan wrote. “Still, Fetterman works in Washington. And there are always other buckets of money. That might explain why Fetterman has broken with Democratic colleagues on developments in artificial intelligence and cryptocurrencies.”
In MS NOW, Zeeshan Aleem said “good riddance” to Fetterman.
“Fetterman did not say whether he would become an independent or join the Republican Party if he were to leave. But his departure from the party in order to support Israel would still be a remarkable development for a politician who was once widely — and, in my opinion, misguidedly — hailed as an exciting exemplar of populist progressivism,” Aleem wrote. “His threat of an exit also reflects how quickly the Democratic Party is reorienting on Israel policy, and growing less hospitable to those who advocate for backing the country’s government unconditionally.”
“Losing a lawmaker in a battleground state would deal a blow to Democrats, who already have to fight tooth and nail for razor-thin majorities in the Senate. Regardless, Fetterman’s warning foreshadows a tectonic shift on the electoral left — and a positive one,” Aleem said. “Ultimately it will be best for the left if Fetterman, who seems to spend more time on Fox News by the day, is replaced by a progressive in Pennsylvania. The Democratic Party cannot re-establish moral authority unless, at a minimum, it looks to put an end to backing Israeli domination of Gaza and observing human rights with consistency.”
- I normally love stories of bipartisan cooperation, but something about what Fetterman’s doing seems off.
- Simple altruism doesn’t explain a person who ran as a progressive fully endorsing his Republican counterpart.
- The simplest explanation is that Fetterman is being negatively polarized against his party by progressives.
On paper, John Fetterman just delivered so much of what I dream of.
A Democratic politician showed up at Republicans’ midterm convention with a simple message: My Republican counterpart is good at his job. He is worthy of office. I don’t hate him — in fact, we’re friends — and he delivers for his constituents. I’ll work with the Republican president because I love America and I want to get things done for my state, and it doesn’t matter that I have a D next to my name and they have Rs next to theirs.
Is this the return to decency I’ve predicted? A politician who can win widespread support from the other party? A senator in an actually competitive swing state not afraid to cross party lines?
My heart!
Well, not quite.
In reality, everything about Fetterman’s actions is perplexing — if not frustrating — to me. What really happened, it seems, is a politician ran on one set of issues, and then, in one of the most peculiar turns I can remember, became singularly focused on something that has nothing to do with any of them.
Fetterman, you’ll remember, campaigned in 2022 as a kind of working-class everyman. The hoodie-wearing, jean-short-rocking townie from Braddock, Pennsylvania, reminded me of so many friends I grew up with in Bucks County or went to college with in Pittsburgh. He exuded Pennsylvania. He felt authentic. His politics were progressive, yes, but he didn’t rely on academic jargon; instead, he connected his beliefs to his experience living in a Pennsylvania town that had been hollowed out and destroyed the way so many others had.
It’s hard to remember now, but these were his 2022 campaign priorities: a minimum wage increase, marijuana legalization, healthcare access, criminal justice reform, voting access, and a compassionate immigration system. He built an entire identity around his proximity to union, working class jobs, and he repeatedly signaled that he would focus on what mattered to workers across Pennsylvania who felt like Washington, D.C. had left them behind. He was a new-age Pennsylvanian Bernie Bro.
Of course, Fetterman’s campaign was upended by his stroke, which occurred just before the Democratic primary. And, honestly, nothing has quite felt the same since. As his speech and physical affect diminished, his health became the story. Could Fetterman still do the job? Then, as he slowly rehabilitated, another story took hold: his clinical depression. In February of 2023, he stepped away from the Senate to receive inpatient treatment for depression, leading to another round of questions about the senator’s fitness for office.
And then October 7 happened.
Since Hamas attacked Israel in 2023, Fetterman has made Israel policy one of his top issues. He talks about Israel constantly, and he’s said or implied on multiple occasions that he would leave the Democratic Party if it became “anti-Israel” — which he’s (at times) defined as the national party platform including funding cuts to military support for Israel.
Fetterman is a genuine enigma these days. Interpreting his worldview became harder after his stroke, which damaged his ability to speak and navigate interviews and sometimes makes him difficult to decipher — especially when the conversations include quick back-and-forths. But he certainly seemed to articulate a worldview when Jon Stewart pressed Fetterman about his comments on Israel: Israel was his red line. He could agree with a politician on a whole host of economic issues, like increasing the social safety net or helping labor wrest capital back from corporations, but if they disagreed on Israel, then he didn’t want them in his party.
Stewart — appropriately, in my view — expressed some shock at this. How could this guy who ran on such working-class, progressive bona fides now tell his constituents that he didn’t want people in his party who disagreed with him on one specific foreign policy question, one that didn’t even exist when he was on the campaign trail? It seems like a very bizarre line to draw.
Then, of course, The Wall Street Journal ran its exposé. In a deeply sourced exclusive, The Journal reported that Fetterman has seemed uninterested in the work of being a senator, instead becoming preoccupied with cultivating media relationships and publicly advocating for Israel. They came with receipts: text messages between Fetterman and staffers, constituents recounting their experiences trying to meet with him, and a lot of off-the-record comments from people who worked for him or had been in his office.
In just one of many jarring examples, Fetterman refused to meet with a state lawmaker who wanted to discuss programs for the homeless and working poor. Later that day, he met with former college basketball coach Bruce Pearl, an outspoken Israel advocate, to discuss college sports legislation. When the Senate ledger started logging his absences from hearings and votes, he adopted a new strategy to drop into Senate hearings or votes just long enough to be marked as present before slipping away.
And it all led up to last night: In a heavily edited video address at the Republican National Committee gathering in Dallas, Texas, Fetterman appeared on screen to introduce — and endorse — his Republican counterpart, Sen. Dave McCormick. While Pennsylvania does not have a Senate race this year, it was still rather shocking in a midterm election where Democrats have a real chance to take back the Senate. Standing in front of an old U.S. Steel mill, he told the audience that McCormick “is the kind of senator that gets the job done” before promising to work with President Trump to revitalize manufacturing in Pennsylvania.
Again: It’s all just odd. I’m not exactly sure what Fetterman’s end goal is, and I certainly don’t think his appearance can be reduced to a simple belief in bipartisanship or support of Trump’s (or McCormick’s) performance. After all, the Trump administration has leveled a full-on assault on nearly every priority of Fetterman’s party, including many of the ones he personally advocated for as a candidate. At the same time, manufacturing jobs in Pennsylvania — the very thing Fetterman appeared on screen to stump for — have continued to decline under Trump.
The simplest theory is probably the most likely: Fetterman is being radicalized by negative polarization. He took a hardline pro-Israel stance immediately after October 7, which is understandable since Israel, our ally, had just suffered a 9/11-like event. That stance then drew the ire of the party’s left wing, which made him dig in. So the progressive left dug in, and a whole other war began. Three years later, the volley of negative polarization has run so many cycles that it seems to have reduced him to a single issue. He’s learned that the more he aligns himself with Republicans or reaches across the aisle, the angrier the left gets and the more attention he gets, so he just keeps pressing that button.
If you want my theory, that’s it.
Still, I’ll allow for the possibility that Fetterman is motivated by a desire to model and act on bipartisanship. After all, he still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats, and he continues to assure his party that he will never become a Republican (he released a statement making that assurance again shortly after his RNC appearance). Maybe he’s just reaching across the aisle to build bridges, not to poke the left in the eye. What’s the harm in praising his Republican counterpart? Why does it matter so much if he says “I support Israel unequivocally” and tries to pull his party toward him on that issue? Is any of this all that big a deal?
But it’s a story so simple I don’t think I buy it. Paired with reporting about his obsession with media appearances and indifference to constituent services, he comes across less like a friendly bipartisan warrior and more like a guy who is simply uninterested in doing the job of being a senator; less like a Democrat willing to see the good in Republicans than a Democrat who is reveling in his own intraparty squabbling; and most of all like someone who has forgotten the promises he made to the Pennsylvanians who elected him.

Can you give an update on Russian oil sanctions? I’ve heard that they’ve been lifted to help with the oil squeeze in Iran/Hormuz.
— Jonathan from Omaha, NE
Tangle: After the war began and Iran constricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. announced that it would waive sanctions on Russian oil for a period of 30 days beginning on March 12. This waiver allowed countries to purchase oil on Russian tankers already at sea, but it did not impact new oil shipments. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the move would provide temporary relief as the U.S. navigated the war with Iran.
The initial waiver expired on April 11; however, on April 17, the U.S. extended the waiver for an additional 30 days. It then issued another extension on May 18, reportedly following a request from “energy-vulnerable countries” most impacted by limited oil transport through the Middle East. However, no new extensions have been issued following the third waiver’s expiration on June 17, when the Trump administration was discussing a peace deal with Iran.
In the aftermath of Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-SC) death in July, the Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which is currently under consideration in the House. The bill would impose new sanctions on Russia’s leadership and energy sector, as well as impose sanctions on the “shadow fleet” that Russia has used to circumvent existing international sanctions and grant the executive branch the authority to impose 100% tariffs on importers of Russian oil.

On Wednesday, the Treasury Department announced that it would buy back up to $6 billion of its own long-dated debt, part of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s effort to at least double the department’s regular buyback program to bring down borrowing costs. The Treasury has about $30 trillion in outstanding debt held in Treasury notes, or T-notes, and it purchased back $2 billion of 10–20-year bonds last month. Yields on T-notes have been increasing in recent months, affecting borrowing rates for consumers and companies. However, the department’s announcement underwhelmed the bond market, as the yield on the 10-year T-note rose by 0.05 percentage points on the day to its highest level since October 2023. Katie Pumphrey, an ultra-marathon swimmer and lifelong Maryland resident, had always wanted to swim in the Baltimore Harbor, but pollution and sewage made it unsafe to do so. Over the last decade, however, nonprofit leaders and city officials worked to make the harbor swimmable. Members of the Waterfront Partnership pushed for sewage system upgrades and for more citywide trash cans to prevent added sewage, and an environmental scientist designed a solar- and water-powered machine to gather up 12 dumpsters of trash each day from the harbor. By 2023, the bacteria levels were low enough for a crew of scientists to test out the water, which proved safe. Since then, Pumphrey has swum in the Baltimore Harbor and become the first person to swim the 24 miles from the Chesapeake Bay to the Baltimore Harbor. Pumphrey said, “I felt so proud of Baltimore, and all of the organizations in the city that worked on and continue to work on our harbor.” The Philadelphia Citizen has the story.

For one extraordinary moment on Thursday night, the giant screens at the Republican convention in Dallas did not show another minister in the Trump administration, a Republican member of Congress, or a party candidate. Instead, they showed John Fetterman, the sitting Democratic senator from Pennsylvania.
“Why am I here speaking with you today? Because, well, I am a common-sense Democrat,” Fetterman said in a prerecorded video. “I will always stand with America. I will always reject extremism, socialism, and this anti-American way of life.”
Fetterman appeared in the video with the Mon Valley Works steel plant in western Pennsylvania behind him and devoted most of his remarks to his Senate colleague, Republican Dave McCormick.
“Dave McCormick is the kind of senator who gets things done, and he will fight for Pennsylvania,” he said. “I am proud to call him my friend.”
He then pointed to the steel plant behind him and said, “Right over my shoulder is this iconic American steel plant. And this is exactly the kind of thing that we are going to work together on, and work with President Trump to fight for and protect the steel way of life, right here in the Steel Valley.”
Fetterman presents Republican Senator McCormick as 'great friend'
Then came an introduction rarely heard from a Democratic senator on the stage of the opposing party’s convention.
“I have the opportunity to introduce this great American, a great senator. And yes, he is in a different party, but I am proud to call him a great friend of mine. So for everyone there in Dallas, I am here to introduce Dave McCormick.”
McCormick took the stage and responded with a gesture of his own.
“How great is John Fetterman?” he told the crowd, thanking him for his “friendship” and his “courage.”
Shortly afterward, a White House account shared the video with the caption, “Based John Fetterman.”
“Based” is internet slang used as praise, describing someone who is not particularly concerned about what others think of their views, or a position seen as bold and worthy of admiration because it breaks with convention. In this context, the meaning is roughly that Fetterman says what he thinks and is not afraid to go against the grain.
The episode was especially unusual because Fetterman is not a Republican who switched parties, nor has he announced any intention of doing so. In fact, he repeatedly emphasizes that he remains a Democrat.
He also was not appearing to support a Republican candidate currently running against a Democrat for a Senate seat. McCormick already serves as Pennsylvania’s second Republican senator.
Even so, the sight of a Democratic senator appearing at the Republican convention, while using some of the language the opposing party uses against the Left, made the moment especially striking. Political commentators in the US described it as an “extraordinary escalation” in the widening rift between Fetterman and his party.
His story was unusual long before the night in Dallas.
Fetterman, who stands more than two meters tall and for years was known for wearing hoodies and shorts, with an appearance almost as far removed as possible from the traditional image of a US senator, began his political career as mayor of Braddock, a small, struggling steel town in Pennsylvania.
He was later elected lieutenant governor of the state, and in 2022 ran for the Senate as a figure many associated with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party.
Just days before the Democratic primary that year, Fetterman suffered a stroke. He won the primary and later the general election, although he was left with difficulties processing spoken language.
Another crisis came just months after he entered the Senate. In February 2023, he voluntarily admitted himself to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center for treatment for clinical depression. He later spoke publicly about his mental health struggle and the importance of seeking treatment.
Fetterman comes out in staunch support of Israel after October 7
But the political shift that transformed him from a popular figure on the Left into a deeply controversial one within his party began largely after October 7.
Fetterman came out unequivocally in support of Israel in its war against Hamas, opposed pressure on Israel from parts of the Left, and repeatedly clashed with progressive activists. His support for Israel gradually became one of the clearest fault lines between him and parts of the Democratic Party.
In 2024, he also skipped the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though he said at the time that his decision had nothing to do with political disagreements or Israel.
He said his three children were on summer vacation and that he preferred to spend the four days with them. He said he had made the decision even before the presidential debate in June, which eventually led Joe Biden to withdraw from the race.
Since Trump returned to the White House, the gap between Fetterman and parts of his party has widened further.
He supported several Trump nominees for administration positions, voted alongside Republicans in the fight over the government shutdown, and opposed congressional efforts to end the war in Iran. After Trump’s 2024 election victory, Fetterman became the first Democratic senator to meet with the president-elect at Mar-a-Lago.
Fetterman, however, continues to reject claims that he is on his way to becoming a Republican.
“I am not going to become a Republican, but I am going to be a Democrat who is going to have a conversation with anybody that is acting in good faith,” he said recently.
He also wrote that he would be a “terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with the Democrats.”
He has, however, identified one red line, a situation in which, in his words, the Democratic Party becomes an “anti-Israel party.”
Fetterman support drops sharply among Pennsylvania Democrats
The polling illustrates how dramatically his political standing has changed.
According to an August New York Times poll cited by AP, only about two in 10 registered Democrats in Pennsylvania had a favorable view of Fetterman, compared with 74% in 2024.
Among Republicans in the state, by contrast, 73% viewed him favorably. Senior Democratic officials and activists in Pennsylvania have also said they are not asking him to join them on the campaign trail ahead of the midterm elections.
At the same time, his relationship with McCormick has become especially close. The two appear together at events and have even established a joint political fundraising committee, an unusual step for two senators from rival parties.
That is why the appearance in Dallas amounted to far more than a one-minute video clip.
As the Republican Party held the first midterm election convention of its kind in an effort to energize its voter base ahead of November, it was a Democratic senator who arrived and used some of the same messages Republicans themselves are seeking to put at the center of the campaign, while continuing to insist that he remains in his party.
Fetterman did not announce that he was crossing party lines. Instead, he did something perhaps even harder to fit into Washington’s conventional political categories: He appeared at the opposing party’s convention, praised a Republican senator as his friend, pledged to work with Trump, and in the same breath reminded everyone, “Yes, I am a Democrat.”
